claims.text: The initial alloy is equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
One proposed sample is nearly defect-free and another contains approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The proposed framework integrates first-principles DFT, machine-learning optimization of interatomic force constants, and explicit electron-phonon coupling.
Separately modeling anharmonic phonon scattering, defect interactions, and electronic transport will decouple lattice and electronic thermal conductivity.
Machine-learning refinement will provide a more accurate description of interatomic-force-constant fluctuations and atomic-scale lattice dynamics.
Anharmonic scattering, defect-induced scattering, and electron-phonon interactions materially influence heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
Approximately 1 wt.% oxygen influences thermal transport through defect scattering.
Explicitly accounting for oxygen impurities, anharmonicity, and electron-phonon coupling will outperform perfect-crystal models.
The framework will improve lattice-thermal-conductivity prediction accuracy by approximately 20% relative to earlier Debye- or DFT-derived approaches.
The model will predict experimentally separated lattice thermal conductivity within ±20% from 200 to 1200 K.
Electronic and lattice contributions are comparable below 200 K.
The lattice contribution dominates above 300 K.
Earlier predictive methods represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals.
Earlier methods used Debye approximations or DFT-derived elastic properties.
Earlier methods conflate lattice and electronic transport and inadequately capture atomic-scale complexity.
The hypothesis applies to homogeneous HfNbTaTiZr with or without approximately 1 wt.% oxygen from 200 to 1200 K.
Significant secondary phases or microstructural inhomogeneity may invalidate the model.
Impurity-distribution and microstructural-defect variations may not be fully captured by the model.
Separated thermal-transport measurements can decisively falsify the model if lattice-conductivity errors exceed ±20%.

contradictions.description: The stated applicability range begins at 200 K, but the predicted outcome makes claims for temperatures below 200 K.
The model is limited to 200–1200 K, whereas the proposed validation experiment spans 100–1300 K without distinguishing out-of-domain tests from decisive in-domain comparisons.
A 20% relative improvement over prior approaches and an absolute prediction error below ±20% are different accuracy metrics; the hypothesis presents them as if they quantify the same improvement.

The predicted outcome refers to electron and phonon contributions, while the falsification rule says electron and photon contributions; the latter is inconsistent with the proposed thermal-transport mechanism.
